questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Learn a new word and you will, for the next few days, notice it everywhere: in conversations, on signs, in a book you happen to pick up. The word has not actually become more common overnight. What has changed is your attention: a category that was previously invisible to your filtering attention has just been switched on, and your brain now flags every match instead of letting it pass unnoticed. Researchers call this the frequency illusion, and it applies well beyond words — a newly bought car model, a rare medical term, a friend's unusual surname all seem to multiply the moment we first learn to notice them.

options.text: Why Rare Words Eventually Become Common Usage
The Frequency Illusion: Noticing, Not Multiplying
How Buying a New Car Changes Consumer Behaviour
The Neuroscience of Learning Foreign Vocabulary
Why Attention Filters Cannot Be Consciously Controlled

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb solar radiation throughout the day and release it slowly after sunset, keeping city centres measurably warmer overnight than the surrounding countryside, sometimes by several degrees. This urban heat island effect intensifies with density: a compact downtown of tall buildings and paved surfaces retains far more heat than a suburb with the same population spread across lawns and tree cover. Cities have begun countering the effect with reflective rooftops, rooftop gardens, and strategically planted street trees, each of which reduces the surface temperature enough to measurably lower night-time readings across an entire district.

options.text: why concrete is a more durable building material than asphalt
how urban density and paved surfaces cause cities to retain heat, and how this can be countered
the total energy cost of air conditioning in modern cities
the history of rooftop garden design in urban architecture
comparing suburban and rural population density trends

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: The trillions of bacteria living in the human gut do far more than assist digestion; they train the immune system from infancy, teaching it to distinguish harmless food particles and resident bacteria from genuine threats. Children raised in unusually sterile environments, with minimal early microbial exposure, show measurably higher rates of allergic and autoimmune conditions later in life, a pattern researchers attribute to an immune system that never received enough early "practice" distinguishing friend from foe. The gut microbiome, in this view, functions less like a passive digestive aid and more like an essential training ground for the body's entire defence system.

options.text: methods for treating autoimmune conditions in adults
how early gut microbiome exposure trains the immune system to distinguish threats from harmless particles
the total number of bacterial species found in the human gut
why sterile environments are always preferable for young children
the digestive function of gut bacteria in nutrient absorption

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: As athletes and competitors approach the absolute physical limits of a sport, the gap in raw skill between the best and the merely very good narrows dramatically, and outcomes on any given day come to depend increasingly on factors no one can fully control: a gust of wind, a slightly favourable bounce, a rival's minor lapse in concentration. This is the paradox of skill: precisely because everyone at the top has become so uniformly excellent, luck's share of the outcome does not shrink alongside the shrinking skill gap — it grows to fill the space skill differences used to occupy.

options.text: Luck matters more in sports where competitors have lower overall skill levels.
As competitors' skill levels converge near the top, luck plays an increasingly large role in outcomes.
The most skilled athletes are the ones least affected by chance events during competition.
Improving raw skill is the only reliable way to reduce the influence of luck on an outcome.
Outcomes in elite competition are entirely determined by chance rather than skill.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
For the first year of learning to bake bread, everything I made came out dense and flat, and I blamed my oven, my flour, even my kitchen's altitude before finally admitting the problem was technique. What changed things was forcing myself to weigh every ingredient instead of trusting cups and eyeballed handfuls, and to time each rise by texture rather than the clock. The first properly risen loaf, when it finally came, didn't feel like beginner's luck — it felt like the readable result of finally measuring the right things. I still under-proof a loaf occasionally, but now I know within a few minutes what went wrong, instead of shrugging and blaming the equipment.

Statements
(a) The writer initially attributed her failures to her equipment and environment rather than her technique.
(b) Switching to weighing ingredients was one of the key changes that improved her results.
(c) She now judges dough readiness primarily by the clock rather than by texture.
(d) Her first successful loaf felt like an unrepeatable stroke of luck.
(e) She can now usually identify what went wrong when a loaf under-proofs.
(f) She no longer makes any mistakes when baking bread.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Many oak and beech trees produce enormous seed crops only once every several years, a pattern called masting, rather than a steady moderate crop annually. One explanation holds that masting evolved to overwhelm seed predators: producing so many seeds in a single year that squirrels and insects cannot possibly eat them all, guaranteeing some survive, while producing almost nothing in intervening years starves predator populations back down. A second, competing explanation attributes masting instead to shared weather cues: trees across a region synchronise flowering only when a particular spring temperature threshold is met, and heavy seed years simply reflect years when conditions for pollination happened to be unusually favourable for every tree at once.

options.text: The first explanation proposes that masting overwhelms predators through occasional very large seed crops.
The first explanation suggests that lean years help reduce seed predator populations.
The second explanation attributes synchronised masting to a shared weather-based cue.
The second explanation agrees with the first that masting evolved specifically to starve predator populations.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same pattern of irregular, synchronised seed production.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the underlined phrase "functional fixedness"?
questions.context: Handed a candle, a box of tacks, and a book of matches, and asked to attach the candle to a wall so it can burn without dripping wax on the floor below, most people struggle, fixated on the box only as a container for the tacks. The solution — tack the box itself to the wall as a small shelf — eludes them not because it is difficult, but because the box's conventional role as "a container" blocks them from seeing its equally available role as "a flat surface." Psychologists call this _functional fixedness_: a tendency to perceive an object only in terms of its most familiar use.

options.text: a physical inability to manipulate small objects such as tacks or boxes
a preference for solving problems as quickly as possible, even carelessly
a difficulty perceiving alternative uses for an object beyond its familiar function
a fixed, unchangeable belief about how candles should be mounted on walls
the tendency for problems involving fire to be solved more slowly than others

questions.context: A forager honeybee returning from a rich flower patch performs a figure-eight waggle dance on the vertical comb inside the hive, its body vibrating along the dance's central straight run. The angle of that run relative to straight up encodes the direction of the food source relative to the sun, while the duration of the vibration encodes distance: longer runs signal food farther away. Other bees crowd around the dancer, tracking the pattern in the dark hive interior largely by touch and the vibrations transmitted through the comb, then depart directly for a patch they have never personally visited.

( ③ ) Some productivity techniques exploit this directly, encouraging people to jot down an unfinished task's next concrete step, which appears to satisfy enough of the "open loop" to quiet the intrusive recall.
